segments.text: Hello and welcome to this week's Health Report with me, Norman Swan. Today, should parents delay their child's surgery because the anaesthetic might damage future school performance? Is there really as much vitamin D deficiency around as some people say? With women living longer and longer after a diagnosis of breast cancer, what support do they need? And new and troubling findings about drug-caused deaths amongst healthcare professionals.
There's been lots of research suggesting that doctors and others are at increased risk of suicide because of the stressful work,
perhaps the kind of person attracted to those professions, and the access to dangerous medications.
But until this study from the Department of Forensic Medicine at Monash University,
not much has been known about Australian healthcare professionals,
much less the full range, including paramedics, nurses and vets, as well as doctors and dentists.
And some of the results are quite surprising.
The lead researcher was Jennifer Pilgrim.
We looked at deaths reported to an Australian coroner between 2003 and 2013,
where the death was caused by drugs and involved a healthcare professional.
And what did you find?
We found 404 deaths.
Most of these involved intentional self-harm or suicide and also mental illness.
And professional and personal stresses were also very common.
So financial problems, relationship problems, workplace stress, those sorts of things.
These are cases that came to the coroner?
Yes, that's right. So these are all deaths that were reported to the coroner.
And have you any sense of what goes beyond that?
How many you might have missed that don't go to the coroner but might be deaths that are self-harm?
All deaths that are unnatural or unexpected are reported to an Australian coroner.
So it should have captured all of these sorts of deaths, but obviously it doesn't capture any of the living cases of drug abuse and intent to self-harm in this population.
So near misses and so on.
Yeah.
What numbers did you come up with?
So there were 404 deaths altogether.
Most of these involved females and nurses.
the rate of deaths which takes into account the number of people employed in these professions
in australia was highest for the veterinarian group and most of these vets involved intentional
self-harm where they took an excessive amount or an overdose of barbiturates which are drugs
commonly used in animal euthanasia did nurses come up top because there are far more nurses
than any other health care profession in australia or exactly yeah i mean there were more
cases involving nurses. However, when we broke this down and put it in proportion of the number
of nurses, as well as the other occupations working in these professions across Australia,
that's where the vets came up on top. So the veterinarian group was smaller, but in proportion
to the number of vets employed in Australia, the rate was highest for vets.
So let's dissect the gender split. So is it more women than men because of the numbers of nurses
or that showed up in veterinarians as well?
There were more females in the cohort overall,
but obviously nursing is dominated by females
and that was the largest category.
So when we looked at the doctors and other medical practitioners,
men were highest in this group.
So I think the number of females is just the over-representation of females in nursing.
Before we get to the causes,
it's been often said that anaesthetists are a very common group
within the medical profession who take their own lives.
Is that true in this group?
We did find a high mortality rate for the anesthesiology group
and most of these involved taking the anesthetic drugs from work.
And what about nursing specialty?
Did you manage to dissect that further?
Because of the coding on the National Cronial Information System database
which we used for this research, some was more specific than others
so we just looked at the nursing group as a whole.
There were some that were more specific that we could break down into the different groups,
but we tended just to look at the group as a whole.
Now, this contradicts the national trend in suicide, does it not?
I mean, suicide, commoner in young males, commoner in elderly males,
and there's kind of a hollowed out group in the middle,
but generally completed suicide is more common in men than in women.
And you're turning up women.
What's going on here?
Well, that's a very good question.
I think that it obviously is still a problem in women, perhaps in the healthcare professional industry specifically.
So again, we had more women in this group because of the number of women in nursing.
But I guess it just raises the issue of suicide in this group among females in this industry more specifically and why we need more research in this space.
And with nurses, it was access to the means as well as vets and anaesthetists and others?
We found in about a fifth of the cases overall, the healthcare professionals were accessing the
drugs from work. So that included some nurses, but that was looked as an overall figure.
And of course, this was where this had actually been described in the coroner's findings. So
it may have actually been an underestimation of the true number of cases where people were
accessing drugs from work. Now, suicide is incredibly complicated. It's not necessarily
always related to mental health issues.
It can be impulsive.
It can be for all sorts of reasons.
How good were the coroners in identifying what they thought were the key factors leading
to that person taking his or her own life?
Well, that's something I probably won't be able to comment on.
Actually, I'm not an expert in suicide or coroner's findings, so I might just leave
that one for somebody else, I think.
But the factors the coroners did identify were what?
Yeah, so the coroners, it sort of varies in cases and also the coding of intentional
self-harm on the National Coronial Information System database is actually performed by coders
interpreting the coronial findings. So in your view, do these data, it's small numbers, but each
one represents a major tragedy for the person and their loved ones around them. Does it tell you
anything about prevention? Well, I think one of the key findings of this study in terms of prevention
was that healthcare professionals are not exempt from mental illness and substance abuse problems.
I think that it would be easy to assume that they are exempt from mental health and substance abuse problems,
but they're just like everybody else.
And what the research around the world shows us is that many healthcare professionals are afraid to talk up
and speak up about their problems from the fear of stigmatisation and potentially losing their jobs.
So many healthcare professionals either treat themselves or seek very private treatment
or don't seek treatment at all.
So it just highlights the need for better detection
of these problems among healthcare professionals
in order to provide them with the support that they need.
And do you have a theory about vets?
I don't actually.
Our study didn't look into why vets were overrepresented
in terms of intentional self-harm,
but other studies have explored the high prevalence
of certain occupations in drug abuse and intentional self-harm
and basically what they say is we're not really sure what the answer is,
whether it's environmental factors such as access to controlled drugs and workplace stress,
whether they're bigger contributors to this issue
or whether certain individuals with a predisposition for drug abuse seek out these professions.
There is a bit of evidence that if you make it harder to get a hold of a gun
or you put up a fence on a spot where people traditionally have jumped from,
you do actually make a difference to the rates.
And then when you actually save people from an intention
which would have definitely resulted in their death,
often there's regret and relief that in fact they were saved.
What about restricting access to the means?
That's really a question for the workplace and industries
and relevant regulation agencies for these professions.
I can't comment on access to drugs,
But we're hopeful that this research helps to inform those policies and helps to open up those avenues for discussion.
Jennifer, thank you for joining us on The Health Report.
You're welcome.
Jennifer Pilgrim is in the Department of Forensic Medicine at Monash University in Melbourne.
And you're listening to The Health Report here on RN, ABC News Radio and CBC Radio across Canada.
Until the government changed the rules, making vitamin D tests less enticing for doctors to order,
Australian taxpayers were spending hundreds of millions of dollars a year on investigations which were mostly of little value.
It was fuelled a little bit by a panic generated by the belief that vitamin D deficiency was rife in the community,
despite all the sun shining on this big brown land.
And now an article in the prestigious New England Journal of Medicine
has suggested that the case for widespread vitamin D deficiency,
at least in North America, has been overblown.
One of the authors is Professor Patsy Brannan
from the Department of Nutritional Sciences at Cornell University.
Dr. Brannan is speaking here to Joel Werner,
who wanted to know how vitamin D deficiency shows itself.
Vitamin D deficiency is most recognized by its adverse impact on bone health.
So the deficiency in children can result in a condition known as rickets,
and in adults it can result in a condition known as osteomalacia.
In both conditions, the bones are not well mineralized,
so they're not as strong as you would like them to be.
But these symptoms only manifest in the most severe cases of vitamin D deficiency.
How do we measure vitamin D deficiency more generally?
The way that we measure it is by measuring the amount of metabolite, a form of vitamin D in our blood known as 25-hydroxy vitamin D.
And that tells us about not only the vitamin D that you get from your diet, but the vitamin D that you make in your skin when you're exposed to sunlight.
So that 25-hydroxy-D is really important for telling us what a person's complete exposure to vitamin D is.
But in an article you recently wrote in the New England Journal of Medicine,
you suggest that maybe the way we've been measuring vitamin D has problems.
Can you dig into that a little bit for us?
So it's not so much the measurement, it's how we interpret that measurement.
for this 25-hydroxy-D, how much of it is too little and indicative of being at risk for too
little vitamin D or being vitamin D deficient, and how much of it is the right amount to have.
So if you have your vitamin D measured at your doctor's office, they're going to tell you,
are you in the right range or do you have too little and are you at risk of being deficient?
And the controversy has been, how do you judge, how do you interpret that 25-hydroxy-D?
So in the United States and in other places, people have been using values of more than 15 animals per liter is optimal.
And what they've been interpreting then is anyone with values less than 15 animals per liter is deficient.
And our article is about why that is not the best way to assess whether somebody has enough vitamin D or too little vitamin D.
And so why isn't that the best way to interpret these figures?
Part of it gets at how you interpret the recommendations that were made in the United States and Canada for how much vitamin D our healthy population needs.
and what that amount that's recommended is it meets the needs of almost everybody in the population,
97.5% of the people in the population.
So in a way of thinking about how much nutrient you need,
it also means that some of our population needs less than that.
So if you use that as a cut point, if you say less than 15 nanomoles per liter is deficient,
you're overestimating the prevalence of deficiency in your population.
And I mean, the title of your article asks the question, is there really a pandemic?
So you're saying that by interpreting the measurements the way that we have,
we may have been overestimating the idea that there is a vitamin D deficiency.
We might be, yes.
Based on the way that the recommended amounts were determined in North America for U.S. and Canada,
what we would want to look at is the number of people in our healthy population
who have 25 hydroxy-B levels, less than 14 nanomoles per liter.
That becomes a much smaller number.
So, for example, in the U.S., that's only 13% of our adults, not more than 30% of our adults.
But what are the implications of not getting this right?
I mean, can you describe why this is actually a problem?
There's emerging evidence that there may be individuals that have too much vitamin D.
So we're seeing what's been referred to as a U-shaped risk,
so that people who have very low vitamin D levels in their blood
are at risk for adverse bone health outcomes.
But now we are seeing evidence that people with higher levels of 25-hydroxy D in their blood
may be at risk for some cancers like pancreatic cancer, for an increased rate of falls. So now
there's a concern that we be in, if you will, what we like to call in the US, the sweet spot,
so that we don't have too little, but we don't have too much.
So what recommendation would you offer our listener out there who's taking in this information,
is saying, okay, I can have too much vitamin D, I can have too little vitamin D, but what's the
best advice that you'd give to someone who's concerned about their level of vitamin D?
So that's a really great question. In Australia, you don't have a lot of foods that are fortified
with vitamin D. I think it's your low-fat table spreads, the oil-based table spreads,
and margarines, a few dairy products, but not very many. So most of the vitamin D that you get
in Australia is what you make in the sun. And that becomes a concern because we know that UVB
exposure increases your lifetime risk for skin cancer. So there's another trade-off for you that
we're talking about. But also think about and talk with their physician about how they expose
themselves to the sun. So there are some recommendations in Australia about sunlight
exposure, although in the U.S. our dermatologists are adamant that you shouldn't be out in the sun
without sunscreen. So that's a place where I'd say talk to your physician, but look at the labels
and think about what foods you're choosing. And if you're going to take a vitamin D supplement,
and many people do choose to do that, take one that has about 400 to 600 IUs a day,
which would be 10 to 15 micrograms per day. Professor Brannan, thanks for joining us on
the Health Report today. You're welcome. It was a pleasure speaking with you.
Patsy Brannan is in the Department of Nutritional Sciences at Cornell University,
and she was talking to The Health Report's Joel Werner.
There's been a theoretical concern that giving anaesthetics to children,
particularly young children, could be dangerous.
It comes from animal studies, which suggest some brain damage in neonatal animals
when they are exposed to modern anaesthetics.
The question is, is this a real worry when it comes to real human children?
Well, that's been the subject of a very large study in Queensland
performed by Dr. Pia Glatz and her colleagues.
Pia Glatz is in the Department of Anesthesiology and Intensive Care,
mentioned at Kama County Hospital in Sweden.
Welcome to the Health Report.
Thank you very much.
So before you did your study, was there any evidence at all that there was a worry in children?
We have very much evidence.
As you said, many animal studies have shown that all anesthetic drugs we're using currently
are giving, they are neurotoxic.
They give brain damage when we give anesthetic drugs
to rat babies or monkey babies.
And of course, that raises the question
if this is applicable for human babies and children.
And has it ever been studied before you and children
that it raises a concern?
Yes, smaller studies, epidemiological studies,
just as ours.
It's not so easy to do these animal studies
for ethical reasons.
You can't just take a bunch of kids and give them anesthetic drugs and see what happens.
So you have to do it some other way.
So what did you do in your study?
In Sweden, we have unique registers for the healthcare and school systems.
So we looked at all children born in Sweden between 1973 and 1993.
That's about 2 million children.
And we found those who had surgery before age 4.
and then we excluded those who had neurosurgery or serious malformation
surgery or medical diagnosis who we thought might affect cognitive development
and what outcomes were you looking at was it just school performance?
We looked at school grades at age 16 that's when you leave compulsory school in Sweden
And we also, for the boys, looked at intelligence tests, all Swedish boys do when they are 18 and entering the military system here.
So I think you had 33,000 children out of the 2 million who'd had an anesthetic.
What did you find?
We found that those children, compared to healthy children, had 0.41% lower school grades.
It's a statistically significant difference, but it's very, very small.
we also
we also looked at
we also looked at other factors
that can affect school grades
and we found that other factors
affected much more
such as
if you're a boy you have 10% lower school grades
than the girls
and if your mother lacks university education
you have 10% lower school grades
and if you're born in December, you have 6% lower school grades
than if you're born in January.
Is that because you only get one present at Christmas instead of two?
Just being facetious.
So what's the reason for December?
Is that viral infections in pregnancy or what?
No, I'm not sure.
I think you're almost a year younger than your classmates born in January, 11 months.
I think that's the difference.
We can see a clear line.
your grades get lower for every month you are born in february march april it's a little lower
and what about multiple surgeries some children they fall a lot you know need their
fractures pinned or they've got a condition which requires multiple surgeries
we also looked at that in the primary cohort with 33 000 children we had only one surgery
before h4 and no subsequent hospitalization whatever reason and then we also looked at
Those who had multiple surgery before age four, it was 3,000 or 4,000 children.
And they had a little lower, about 1.5% or 1.8% lower school grades than those who did not.
So maybe that's because they had more duration of anesthesia.
And younger children versus older if they were operated on in infancy?
we thought that the youngest must be the most vulnerable but we couldn't find anything
on contrary we found that those who had lower school grades that were those who had their
anesthesia and surgery between 36 and 48 months so we couldn't find that the youngest
zero to six months were more vulnerable and i presume that you corrected for whether the baby
was premature and the condition that they might have had
that might have affected their development?
We have corrected for all factors we could think of.
As I said, Sweden has unique registers.
So we have used how many siblings you have,
what your mother's education is,
if you're a premature born, household incomes,
everything like that.
And just finally, what does that mean then for parents
whose child might need to have an operation?
So I would not be worried at all.
We can see a small, small difference, but it's so very small.
Other factors affect school age much more.
And you also have to take into account what happens if you don't do the surgery.
We never give surgery and anesthesia to a child, and it's absolutely necessary.
And you have to think what happens if you don't do the maybe eye surgery or ear surgery.
That could give other problems.
So common sense prevails.
Pia Glatz, thanks for joining us on The Health Report.
Thanks for having me.
Pia Glatz is in the Department of Anesthetics and Intensive Care
at Carmel County Hospital in Sweden,
and we'll have a link to that paper on The Health Report's website.
One of the great success stories, there aren't that many actually in cancer,
but one of the great success stories in cancer is breast cancer.
And for many women, it's become almost a chronic disease,
so long do they live with the condition.
But that means that they live with the effects of treatment
and perhaps require supportive care, according to an article in today's Medical Journal of Australia.
And here to talk about it is one of the authors of that paper is Professor Fran Boyle from the Mater Hospital in Sydney.
Welcome to the Health Report.
Hi, Norman.
What are the issues that women with breast cancer face that might need support?
Well, I think during treatment, things like hair loss, for instance,
have been quite underestimated by health professionals in terms of the impact they might have on a woman psychologically.
and her coping during treatment.
And that's something that we finally have some means to address
for some women undergoing chemotherapy with scalp cooling.
So that's something that's new and which is widely used in the UK and Europe.
So we're trying to make sure that Australian women get better access to that.
So this is like a cap where they run cold water through it
so that when the chemo is injected in,
the blood vessels are constricted in the scalp
and it doesn't go to the scalp as much as it would otherwise.
That's right.
The hair follicles kind of hibernate and that means that they're less affected by the chemo.
And we know that women, and it's not a vanity thing, it's often about trying to make sure
that strangers in the supermarket don't inspect the contents of your trolley and make suggestions
about organic food or your children don't get distressed at the school gate when you
come to pick them up.
And why aren't we using the skull caps?
Well, in Australia, the funding for them has mainly been provided through donations.
And so that's a way that units are actually applying them.
But they do mean that patients spend more time in the chemotherapy unit.
So if you've got a very busy chemo unit, there's a lot of logistics that have to be
rearranged to make that work.
But we've been working with different hospitals around the country to see if we can solve
problems for them.
And gradually it's spreading.
I mean, a few weeks ago, we were talking about what women should feel entitled to when they've
got breast cancer. And one is breast reconstruction, for example, which they didn't really feel that
way. I mean, surely, are women's entitled to this treatment?
Oh, well, I think it's something that has implications for the economics of actually
making chemotherapy manageable. So each unit needs to work out a way to do that, that
makes sure other patients are not disadvantaged and waiting lists aren't pushed out for other
kinds of cancer, but I think most places in the Northern Hemisphere, it is considered to be a
standard of care. The US has been, of course, slow to discover it, but they're about to find out and
it will become normal. Another area which has been relatively neglected by the cancer community
is sexual wellbeing when you've had breast cancer. I think that's right, Norman. At the first pass
people going through treatment, the biggest concern is survival and making sure that their
treatment is accomplished on time and, you know, they get through that. But many women then say,
well, I thought it was okay to have no libido when I was having chemotherapy or to have vaginal
dryness when I first started my tablets, but you know what, it's six months on and that's still an
issue for me. And it's something that oncologists are probably not the best or perhaps even surgeons
at picking up in their consultations, because again, follow-up consultations tend to focus on
recurrence risk. So this is more than just having had a mastectomy, although that's
increasingly rare in breast cancer. This is the effect of the treatment. And are there
ways of getting around this? Well, we are learning ways to help women with these symptoms. Libido is
obviously a pretty complex concept that it's not just a physical thing, but an emotional thing as
well. But some of the vaginal symptoms do lend themselves to treatment. And also making sure
that women are referred for the right kind of assessment and help with their partners is a
really important thing to pick up on. Now, one of the things that's underestimated
also as time goes on is distress. You think, well, a woman's survived for five years. Surely
she's not distressed. But the distress, anecdotally, when women come back for surveillance and have
their checkup, seems to recur almost to as bad as it was before. I think that having that annual
mammogram, women regularly say, while they're lying, they're having it, they're standing there.
It's like being back at the beginning all over again.
And it's now recognised that that is a form of post-traumatic stress disorder and needs
to be treated psychologically in a similar way.
So recent studies in Australia have shown that a psychological intervention based on
PTSD interventions is helpful for several kinds of cancer patients with what's called
fear of recurrence.
And I would love to see that rolled out in a more systematic way.
So here we are, we're doling out expensive drugs in expensive chemotherapy units.
Women are having treatment, surgical treatment.
So we've had this, I mean, the implication in your article is we've had this narrow focus on medical things,
yet you need this quite significant support infrastructure around women to actually make the breast cancer care more humane and effective.
I think breast cancer has led the way, as you said, in improving survival.
and now most people will not die of breast cancer,
they'll die of something else.
So it's a teachable moment, if you like,
when other aspects of their health can be addressed,
particularly lifestyle factors such as diet and exercise.
But do the bean counters know they've got to pay for it?
Well, I think they prefer not to
because a lot of that needs to be delivered in the community.
It's not really something that's easily delivered
in large public hospitals.
It has to be close to where women live
And so really GPs are going to be people who are in perhaps a better position to refer women to local services.
So it's a work in progress.
It's a work in progress.
And I guess what we're hoping with this article is that we'll draw to attention, particularly of general practitioners, that working together to solve these issues is going to be required.
It's not something that's going to happen just from the oncological community.
Fran, thanks for joining us.
Thanks, Norman.
Fran Boyle is Professor of Medical Oncology and Director of the Patricia Ritchie Centre for Cancer Care and Research at the Mater Hospital in Sydney.
I'm Norman Swan. This has been The Health Report. Hope you can join me next week.
